statement: Which of the following is found in a synchondrosis?

explanation.b: Synchondrosis contains hyaline cartilage between bones.
explanation.a: Fibrocartilage is found in symphysis.
explanation.c: Ligaments belong to fibrous joints.
explanation.d: Meniscus is in synovial joints like knee.
explanation.e: Synovial fluid is not present in cartilaginous joints.

statement: Which of the following is found in a symphysis?

explanation.a: Symphysis contains fibrocartilage (e.g., intervertebral disc, pubic symphysis).
explanation.b: Hyaline cartilage is typical of synchondrosis.
explanation.c: Ligaments are features of fibrous joints.
explanation.d: Meniscus is part of synovial joints.
explanation.e: Synovial fluid is absent in cartilaginous joints.

subject: Anatomy

statement: Meniscus is a wedge-shaped fibrocartilage found in:

explanation.d: The knee joint features medial and lateral crescentic, wedge-shaped fibrocartilage structures called menisci that deepen the articular surfaces of the tibia to shock-absorb and stabilize the joint.
explanation.a: The hip joint contains a fibrocartilaginous acetabular labrum rather than a wedge-shaped meniscus to deepen its socket.
explanation.b: The elbow joint is a pure hinge synovial joint completely devoid of intra-articular fibrocartilaginous menisci.
explanation.c: The shoulder joint utilizes a glenoid labrum made of fibrocartilage to expand its socket cavity, not a meniscus.
explanation.e: The ankle joint relies purely on bony mortise stability and collateral ligaments without any intra-articular meniscus structures.

subject: Anatomy

statement: Which of the following is not a plane joint:

explanation.d: The knee joint is not a plane joint; it is structurally classified as a modified hinge (bicondylar) joint allowing flexion, extension, and limited rotation.
explanation.a: The joints between articular processes of vertebra (zygapophysial joints) are true plane joints that permit gliding movements.
explanation.b: The joints between carpals (intercarpal joints) are classic plane joints where flat bony surfaces slide past one another.
explanation.c: The joints between tarsals (intertarsal joints) are structurally plane joints designed for limited gliding motions during foot inversion and eversion.
explanation.e: The acromioclavicular joint is anatomically classified as a plane synovial joint allowing gliding movements between the acromion and clavicle.

subject: Anatomy

statement: Select incorrect pair:

explanation.d: Sellar joint (wrist joint) is an incorrect pair because the wrist joint is actually an ellipsoid (condylar) joint, while a sellar (saddle) joint describes the 1st carpometacarpal joint.
explanation.a: Hinge joint (knee joint) is considered a correct traditional pairing as the knee functions primarily as a hinge joint.
explanation.b: Pivot joint (atlantoaxial joint) is a correct pairing because the median atlantoaxial joint allows rotational movement around a central bony pivot.
explanation.c: Ellipsoid joint (wrist joint) is a correct pairing because the radiocarpal articulation features an oval condyle fitting into an elliptical cavity.
explanation.e: Ball and socket joint (shoulder joint) is a correct pairing because the spherical head of the humerus articulates with the shallow glenoid cavity.

subject: Anatomy

statement: The autonomic nervous system:

options.a: arises from the spinal cord only.
options.c: has no connection with the adrenal medulla.
options.d: prepares the body for the fight-or-flight response.
options.e: releases acetylcholine from all postganglionic fibers.

explanation.d: The sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system prepares the body for the fight-or-flight response during stress or emergencies.
explanation.a: It arises from both the brainstem (cranial nerves) and the spinal cord.
explanation.b: It controls smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands, whereas skeletal muscles are controlled by the somatic nervous system.
explanation.c: It has a direct connection with the adrenal medulla, where preganglionic sympathetic fibers stimulate epinephrine and norepinephrine release.
explanation.e: It releases norepinephrine from most sympathetic postganglionic fibers, though sweat glands and certain blood vessels receive acetylcholine.

subject: Anatomy

statement: Which of the following is NOT a component of the central nervous system?

explanation.b: A cranial nerve is a peripheral nerve structure that projects outside the brainstem, making it part of the peripheral nervous system rather than the central nervous system.
explanation.a: Basal ganglia are subcortical nuclei located deep within the cerebral hemispheres of the central nervous system.
explanation.c: Glial cell types like oligodendrocytes and astrocytes are resident supporting cells within the central nervous system.
explanation.d: Neuron populations constitute the primary parenchymal and signaling cells found throughout the central nervous system.
explanation.e: Spinal cord is the major infra-tentorial longitudinal column of neural tissue belonging to the central nervous system.

subject: Anatomy

statement: Outermost covering of a nerve is called:

explanation.d: Epineurium is the dense, outermost covering of a nerve that encloses the entire peripheral nerve trunk and shields it from mechanical strain.
explanation.a: Endomysium is the connective tissue sheath surrounding an individual muscle fiber rather than a nerve.
explanation.b: Endoneurium is the delicate connective tissue layer immediately surrounding an individual axon and its Schwann cell.
explanation.c: Epimysium is the fibrous connective tissue envelope that surrounds an entire skeletal muscle.
explanation.e: Perineurium is the specialized connective tissue sheath that bundles groups of axons into distinct nerve fascicles.

subject: Anatomy

statement: A typical spinal nerve is:

explanation.b: A typical spinal nerve is mixed because it carries both somatic sensory afferent fibers entering the cord and somatic motor efferent fibers exiting the cord.
explanation.a: It is not purely motor, as it receives extensive sensory inputs from the periphery via the dorsal root.
explanation.c: It does not carry parasympathetic fibers, as parasympathetic outflow is restricted to certain cranial nerves and sacral spinal segments S2–S4.
explanation.d: It is not purely sensory, as it contains somatic motor axons destined for skeletal muscle innervation.
explanation.e: It is not purely sympathetic, as sympathetic fibers are absent in several spinal levels and only mix with thoracic and upper lumbar nerves.

subject: Anatomy

statement: Select the INCORRECT match of the ganglion and the cranial nerve supplying its preganglionic fibers:

explanation.e: The submandibular ganglion receives its preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the facial nerve (via the chorda tympani), not from the trigeminal nerve, though it hangs suspended from a trigeminal branch (lingual nerve).
explanation.a: Ciliary ganglion is correctly matched because its preganglionic fibers travel via the oculomotor nerve.
explanation.b: Otic ganglion is correctly matched because its preganglionic fibers travel via the glossopharyngeal nerve.
explanation.c: Pterygopalatine ganglion is correctly matched because its preganglionic fibers travel via the facial nerve (greater petrosal nerve).
explanation.d: Submandibular ganglion is correctly matched because its preganglionic fibers travel via the facial nerve.

subject: Anatomy

statement: Nerve fibers are bound in and held together by connective tissue known as the: A. endomysium.

explanation.d: Perineurium is the specific connective tissue sheath that binds, organizes, and holds groups of nerve fibers together into structural bundles called fascicles.
explanation.a: Endomysium is a histological connective tissue component of skeletal muscle fibers, completely absent in peripheral nerve trunks.
explanation.b: Endoneurium is the finer, delicate connective tissue that surrounds a single individual nerve fiber, rather than binding groups of them together.
explanation.c: Epineurium is the outermost dense connective sheath that surrounds the entire nerve trunk, enclosing all individual fascicles.
explanation.e: Sheath of Schwann is a cellular layer of myelin-producing cells that wraps individual axons, not a fibrous connective tissue matrix that binds bundles.

subject: Anatomy

statement: Which of the following layers of the brain contains blood vessels?

explanation.c: Pia mater is a highly vascularized, delicate connective tissue layer that closely adheres to the contours of the brain surface and contains the plexuses of blood vessels supplying the neural tissue.
explanation.a: Arachnoid mater is a non-vascular, thin, avascular membrane that acts as a barrier barrier layer.
explanation.b: Dura mater contains large venous sinuses and meningeal vessels, but it is a thick, protective dural envelope covering the brain rather than a layer embedded with nutrient brain capillaries.
explanation.d: Subarachnoid space contains CSF and large blood vessel trunks traversing it, but it is an anatomical fluid space rather than a structural tissue layer of the brain itself.
explanation.e: Subdural space is a narrow, potential space between the dura and arachnoid maters that contains a film of fluid but lacks structural blood vessels under normal conditions.

explanation.b: Metacarpals are also long bones but were not the keyed option in this item.
explanation.d: Tarsals are short bones forming ankle support structures.
explanation.e: Vertebrae are irregular bones specialized for spinal protection.

statement: Viable fetus is characterized by all of the following except:

explanation.a: Amniotic fluid volume fluctuates and is not used as a standardized metric or baseline anatomical parameter to define a viable fetus.
explanation.b: A crown-heel length > 250 mm is a standard physical dimension indicative of a fetus that has reached the age of viability.
explanation.c: A crown-rump length > 200 mm corresponds to a gestational milestone where fetal organs are sufficiently developed to support extrauterine life.
explanation.d: A foot length > 40 mm is a highly reliable baseline structural measurement correlated with a viable fetus.
explanation.e: A weight > 500g is the globally recognized statutory weight threshold used to distinguish a viable fetus from an abortion.

subject: Embryology

statement: When does surfactant production start:

explanation.b: Type II pneumocytes initiate secretory differentiation and begin surfactant production around the 24th week of gestation.
explanation.a: At the 21th week, the terminal sacs are still forming, and the respiratory epithelium has not yet initiated surfactant production.
explanation.c: By the 28th week, surfactant production has already been established for several weeks, allowing for viable extrauterine respiration.
explanation.d: The 32nd week represents a period of accelerating surfactant synthesis, well past its initial starting point.
explanation.e: The 36th week marks the approach of term maturation where surfactant production reaches peak quantities, not its inception.

subject: Embryology

statement: Average weight of a fetus at age of 9th month of gestation.

explanation.c: The standard, average weight of a healthy full-term fetus during the 9th month of gestation ranges tightly around 3.0 kg to 3.4 kg.
explanation.a: A weight of 1.5 kg is characteristic of a premature fetus at roughly 30 weeks of gestation, not a full-term 9th month fetus.
explanation.b: A weight of 2.0 kg indicates either a severely growth-restricted fetus or an infant born prematurely around the 8th month.
explanation.d: A weight of 4.0 kg is significantly above average and borders on fetal macrosomia rather than representing the standard average weight.
explanation.e: A weight of 5.0 kg represents extreme macrosomia, typically seen in uncontrolled maternal diabetes, and is not a normal average weight.

subject: Embryology

statement: Fetal period extends from:

explanation.b: The fetal period is strictly defined embryologically as extending from the beginning of the 9th week of development until term birth.
explanation.a: The 7th week to term includes a portion of the embryonic period, during which primary organogenesis is still actively occurring.
explanation.c: The 12th week to term omits the critical transition weeks (weeks 9 through 11) that mark the definitive start of the fetal period.
explanation.d: The 14th week to term represents the early second trimester and misses the entire early developmental phase of the fetal period.
explanation.e: Fertilization to term encompasses the entire prenatal development span, including the pre-embryonic and embryonic stages.

subject: Embryology

statement: Head gains half of the CRL in which week of development:

explanation.b: At the beginning of the fetal period in the 09th week, the head is disproportionately large and constitutes exactly half of the crown-rump length (CRL).
explanation.a: During the 08th week, the embryo is finishing organogenesis and the head-to-body proportion has not yet perfectly equilibrated to the half-CRL ratio.
explanation.c: By the 10th week, body growth begins to accelerate, meaning the head starts to constitute slightly less than half of the total CRL.
explanation.d: In the 11th week, the growth of the limbs and trunk outpaces the head, reducing the head's proportion relative to the crown-rump length.
explanation.e: By the 12th week, head size has decreased further in proportion, making up about one-third of the total crown-rump length instead of half.

statement: A normal somatic cell contains a total of 46 chromosomes. What is the normal complement of chromosomes found in sperm?

explanation.b: Sperm are haploid gametes containing 22 autosomes plus a sex chromosome (X or Y).
explanation.a: 22 autosomes alone omits the required sex chromosome.
explanation.c: 23 autosomes excludes the sex chromosome and gives an incorrect autosomal count.
explanation.d: 23 autosomes plus a sex chromosome would total 24 chromosomes.
explanation.e: 46 chromosomes plus a sex chromosome is diploid and abnormal for sperm.

subject: Embryology

statement: Time taken for spermatogenesis:

explanation.d: Spermatogenesis requires approximately 74 days for complete maturation from spermatogonia to spermatozoa.
explanation.a: 24 days is far shorter than the normal spermatogenic cycle.
explanation.b: 48 days is insufficient for full meiotic and maturational processes.
explanation.c: 60 days underestimates the duration of spermatogenesis.
explanation.e: 90 days exceeds the standard physiologic duration.

subject: Embryology

statement: Which of the following describes the number of chromosomes and amount of DNA in a gamete?

explanation.a: Gametes are haploid cells containing 23 chromosomes and 1N DNA content.
explanation.b: 2N DNA content is characteristic of diploid somatic cells.
explanation.c: 4N DNA content occurs after DNA replication before meiotic division.
explanation.d: 46 chromosomes represents a diploid complement, not a gamete.
explanation.e: 46 chromosomes with 2N DNA describes normal somatic cells.

subject: Embryology

statement: Male is infertile if sperm count is less than:

explanation.b: 20 million/mL is near the lower normal range in older standards.
explanation.c: 40 million/mL is generally considered fertile.
explanation.d: 60 million/mL is well within normal fertility parameters.
explanation.e: 80 million/mL represents a high normal sperm count.

subject: Embryology

statement: Which chromosome composition in a sperm normally results in the production of a genetic female if fertilization occurs?

explanation.a: Fertilization by a sperm containing 22 autosomes plus an X chromosome produces an XX genetic female.
explanation.b: A Y chromosome-bearing sperm produces a genetic male.
explanation.c: 23 autosomes plus an X chromosome gives an incorrect chromosome number.
explanation.d: 23 autosomes plus a Y chromosome incorrectly totals 24 chromosomes.
explanation.e: 23 homologous pairs describes diploid somatic cells, not sperm.

subject: Embryology

statement: All primary oocytes are formed by:

explanation.b: All primary oocytes are formed by month 5 of fetal life after oogonia enter meiosis I.

explanation.c: Puberty initiates ovulation, not formation of primary oocytes.
explanation.d: Week 4 is too early for completion of primary oocyte formation.
explanation.e: Week 8 precedes the peak period of oocyte development.

explanation.c: Formation of primary spermatocytes begins at puberty when spermatogenesis starts.
explanation.a: Spermatogenesis is inactive at birth.
explanation.b: Menopause is a female reproductive event unrelated to spermatocyte formation.
explanation.d: Month 5 of fetal life pertains to oogenesis, not spermatogenesis.
explanation.e: Week 4 of embryonic life is too early for spermatocyte formation.

explanation.b: 20 million is substantially below average ejaculate counts.
explanation.c: 35 million is lower than expected for a normal fertile male.
explanation.e: 500 million exceeds the usual average ejaculate count.

explanation.d: A primary spermatocyte has undergone DNA replication before meiosis I and therefore contains 4N DNA.
explanation.a: 1N DNA content is characteristic of mature gametes.
explanation.b: 2N refers to chromosome number, not replicated DNA quantity in primary spermatocytes.
explanation.c: 3N is not a normal meiotic DNA state.
explanation.e: 8N DNA content does not occur in normal spermatogenesis.

explanation.c: During fetal life, oogonia enter meiosis I and replicate DNA to become primary
explanation.a: At birth, primary oocytes are already formed and arrested.
explanation.b: Puberty resumes maturation but does not initiate meiosis I.
explanation.d: Fertilization completes meiosis II, not formation of primary oocytes.
explanation.e: Ovulation releases a secondary oocyte, not a primary oocyte.

statement: Where do primordial germ cells initially develop?

options.c: In the yolk sac at month 5.
options.d: In the yolk sac at week 4.
options.e: In the yolk sac at week 8.

explanation.d: Primordial germ cells initially develop in the yolk sac near week 4 before migrating to the gonads.
explanation.a: Germ cells migrate to gonads later and do not originate there at month 5.
explanation.b: Gonadal colonization occurs after initial yolk sac development.
explanation.c: Month 5 is far beyond the period of primordial germ cell origin.
explanation.e: Week 8 is later than the initial appearance of primordial germ cells.

subject: Embryology

statement: A young female refused X-rays due to primary oocytes being vulnerable because they are arrested in a stage of meiosis I called:

explanation.c: Primary oocytes remain arrested in the diplotene stage of prophase I from fetal life until ovulation, making them vulnerable to radiation damage.
explanation.a: Anaphase is not the prolonged arrest stage of primary oocytes.
explanation.b: Diakinesis occurs later in prophase I and is not the arrested phase maintained for years.
explanation.d: Metaphase arrest characterizes secondary oocytes, not primary oocytes.
explanation.e: Telophase is a brief meiotic phase and not the long arrest stage.

subject: Embryology

statement: Webbed neck and gonadal dysgenesis are the characteristic findings of?

explanation.e: Turner syndrome classically presents with webbed neck due to cystic hygroma and gonadal dysgenesis causing streak ovaries and primary amenorrhea.
explanation.a: Down syndrome is characterized by trisomy 21 with intellectual disability and epicanthic folds, not gonadal dysgenesis.
explanation.b: Edwards syndrome presents with clenched fists and rocker-bottom feet rather than webbed neck with streak gonads.
explanation.c: Klinefelter syndrome causes testicular atrophy and tall stature in males, not webbed neck.
explanation.d: Patau syndrome is associated with cleft lip/palate and holoprosencephaly, not gonadal dysgenesis.

subject: Embryology

statement: Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 is known as?

explanation.b: Cri-du-chat syndrome results from deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p deletion) causing a characteristic cat-like cry.
explanation.a: Angelman syndrome is caused by maternal deletion of chromosome 15q affecting UBE3A.
explanation.c: Miller-Dieker syndrome is associated with chromosome 17p deletion causing lissencephaly.
explanation.d: Prader-Willi syndrome involves paternal deletion or maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15.
explanation.e: Williams syndrome is due to deletion on chromosome 7 involving the elastin gene.

subject: Embryology

statement: Fetal sex can be diagnosed by noting the presence or absence of the Barr body in cells obtained from the amniotic fluid. What is the etiology of the Barr body?

explanation.c: The Barr body represents inactivation of one X chromosome in female somatic cells.
explanation.a: Inactivation of both X chromosomes would be lethal to the cell.
explanation.b: Homologous chromosome inactivation does not define a Barr body.
explanation.d: Y chromosomes do not form Barr bodies.
explanation.e: Two Y chromosomes are not normally present and do not undergo Barr body formation.

subject: Embryology

statement: Genetic sex is determined at time of:

explanation.b: Genetic sex is established at fertilization when an X- or Y-bearing sperm fertilizes the oocyte.
explanation.a: Birth reveals phenotypic sex but does not determine chromosomal sex.
explanation.c: Implantation occurs after chromosomal sex has already been established.
explanation.d: Ovulation releases only an X-bearing oocyte and cannot determine sex.
explanation.e: Parturition occurs long after genetic sex determination.

subject: Embryology

statement: Most common condition associated with spontaneous abortion:

explanation.a: Chromosomal anomalies are the leading cause of early pregnancy loss.
explanation.b: Ectopic pregnancy is implantation disorder, not cause of spontaneous abortion.
explanation.c: Diabetes increases risk but is not most common cause.
explanation.d: Maternal imprinting disorders are rare causes.
explanation.e: Paternal imprinting disorders are also rare and not primary cause.

subject: Embryology

statement: Webbed neck & gonadal dysgenesis are the characteristic findings of:

explanation.e: Turner syndrome (45,X) causes gonadal dysgenesis (streak ovaries) and webbed neck due to lymphatic developmental abnormalities.
explanation.a: Down syndrome presents with intellectual disability, epicanthic folds, and congenital heart defects, not gonadal dysgenesis.
explanation.b: Edward syndrome (trisomy 18) shows clenched fists and rocker-bottom feet, not webbed neck or gonadal dysgenesis.
explanation.c: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) causes testicular atrophy but not classic webbed neck with gonadal dysgenesis.
explanation.d: Noonan syndrome may show webbed neck but has normal karyotype and no gonadal dysgenesis.

subject: Embryology

statement: Mental deficiency, retarded growth, slanting eyes, small ears, neural tube defects & cardiac defects are the characteristic findings in:

explanation.c: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) presents with intellectual disability, upward slanting eyes, small ears, and congenital heart defects.
explanation.a: Trisomy 13 causes holoprosencephaly and cleft lip/palate rather than typical Down facial pattern.
explanation.b: Trisomy 18 causes micrognathia and clenched hands rather than slanted eyes and classic cardiac features of Down syndrome.
explanation.d: Turner syndrome causes short stature and gonadal dysgenesis, not mental deficiency with craniofacial anomalies.
explanation.e: Klinefelter syndrome causes hypogonadism and learning difficulty but not dysmorphic facial features.

subject: Embryology

statement: Deletion of short arm of chromosome 5 is known as:

explanation.b: Cri-du-chat syndrome results from 5p deletion causing cat-like cry, microcephaly, and intellectual disability.
explanation.a: Angelman syndrome is due to 15q11–q13 maternal deletion/imprinting defect.
explanation.c: Miller-Dieker syndrome involves 17p deletion causing lissencephaly.
explanation.d: Prader-Willi syndrome involves paternal 15q deletion with obesity and hypotonia.
explanation.e: Williams syndrome involves 7q11.23 deletion with “elfin facies.”

subject: Embryology

statement: The main deformity of fetal alcohol syndrome is?

explanation.c: Fetal alcohol syndrome most prominently causes intellectual disability due to alcohol-induced neurodevelopmental injury.
explanation.a: Cataract is more strongly associated with congenital rubella syndrome than fetal alcohol syndrome.
explanation.b: Cleft lip is not the principal deformity associated with prenatal alcohol exposure.
explanation.d: Micrognathia may occur but is not the major manifestation of fetal alcohol syndrome.
explanation.e: Thymic aplasia is characteristic of DiGeorge syndrome, not fetal alcohol syndrome.

subject: Embryology

statement: High level of hCG is found in:

explanation.b: Hydatidiform mole causes excessive trophoblastic proliferation with markedly elevated hCG levels.
explanation.a: Ectopic pregnancy usually has lower and abnormally rising hCG levels rather than extremely high values.
explanation.c: Placenta accreta is abnormal placental adherence without trophoblastic overproduction of hCG.
explanation.d: Placenta previa causes painless bleeding but not marked hCG elevation.
explanation.e: Sacrococcygeal teratoma is a germ cell tumor not characteristically associated with high hCG.

subject: Embryology

statement: Best indicator for assessment of fetal age in first trimester:

explanation.c: Crown-rump length provides the lowest biological variation and the most precise ultrasound estimation of fetal age during the first trimester.
explanation.a: Amniotic fluid amount varies widely due to maternal and placental factors and is never used as an indicator to assess gestational age.
explanation.b: Biparietal diameter is an ultrasound metric reserved for the assessment of fetal age in the second and third trimesters.
explanation.d: Femur length is utilized to calculate fetal growth and gestational age exclusively in the later trimesters, not the first trimester.
explanation.e: Head circumference is an anthropometric parameter used to track development in the second and third trimesters.

subject: Embryology

statement: The ultrasound marker measured before 12 weeks of gestation to assess fetal gestational age is:

explanation.c: Crown-rump length is the definitive biometric parameter measured via ultrasound before 12 weeks of gestation for accurate pregnancy dating.
explanation.a: Abdominal circumference is a metric used primarily in the second and third trimesters to monitor fetal growth and asymmetric restriction, not early age.
explanation.b: Biparietal diameter cannot be reliably measured or used for precise age estimation before the cranial bones mature post-12 weeks.
explanation.d: Femur length is an indicator of skeletal growth that is only measured after the long bones ossify sufficiently during the second trimester.
explanation.e: Head circumference is utilized to evaluate cranial development and fetal age exclusively during the second and third trimesters.

subject: Embryology

statement: Chorionic villus sampling is done at which week:

explanation.d: Chorionic villus sampling is typically performed at 8–9 weeks of gestation.
explanation.a: 12–14 weeks is later than the optimal CVS window.
explanation.b: 14–16 weeks is outside the early diagnostic window.
explanation.c: 16–20 weeks is used for other prenatal tests like amniocentesis timing range.
explanation.e: 10–12 weeks is slightly later than the standard earliest CVS window

subject: Embryology

statement: The main deformity of alcohol fetal syndrome is:

explanation.c: Fetal alcohol syndrome primarily causes intellectual disability due to alcohol-induced neurodevelopmental brain damage.
explanation.a: Cleft lip may occur but is not the defining or main deformity.
explanation.b: Cataract & glaucoma are not typical primary features of fetal alcohol exposure.
explanation.d: Microphthalmia can occur but is not the principal deformity.
explanation.e: Thymic aplasia is characteristic of DiGeorge syndrome, not fetal alcohol syndrome.

explanation.a: Where does the blastocyst implant in placenta Previa:

subject: Embryology

statement: Individual blastomeres were isolated from a blastula at the 4-cell stage. Each blastomere was cultured in vitro to the blastocyst stage and individually implanted into four pseudo-pregnant foster mothers. Which of the following would you expect to observe 9 months later:

options.a: birth of four genetically different babies.
options.b: birth of four genetically identical babies.
options.c: birth of four phenotypically abnormal babies.
options.e: birth of two genetically identical babies.

explanation.b: Blastomeres separated at the 4-cell stage are totipotent and derive from the same zygote, producing four genetically identical babies.
explanation.a: Different genetic makeup occurs in dizygotic twinning, not from one zygote split at cleavage stages.
explanation.c: Early isolated blastomeres can develop normally and are not inherently phenotypically abnormal.
explanation.d: Each implanted blastomere can independently form a viable embryo, not just one.
explanation.e: Separation of all four blastomeres would yield four identical offspring, not only two.

subject: Embryology

statement: Which event occurs during cleavage of the zygote in week 1 of development?

explanation.a: Cleavage produces progressively smaller blastomeres without increasing overall embryonic size.
explanation.b: Cytoplasmic volume does not increase during cleavage divisions.
explanation.c: Blastomeres remain relatively undifferentiated during early cleavage.
explanation.d: Cleavage consists of mitotic, not meiotic, divisions.
explanation.e: The zona pellucida thins before hatching rather than thickening.

subject: Embryology

statement: Where does fertilization occur?

explanation.a: Fertilization most commonly occurs in the ampulla, the widest segment of the uterine tube.
explanation.b: The cervix serves as a passageway for sperm but is not the site of fertilization.
explanation.c: The infundibulum captures the oocyte but is not the usual fertilization site.
explanation.d: The isthmus mainly transports the zygote toward the uterus.
explanation.e: The myometrium is the muscular uterine wall and has no role in fertilization.

subject: Embryology

statement: Where does the blastocyst normally implant?

explanation.c: The blastocyst normally implants in the functional layer of the endometrium.
explanation.a: The basal layer regenerates the endometrium and is not the implantation
explanation.b: Implantation in the cervix is abnormal and ectopic.
explanation.d: The myometrium is the muscular uterine wall, not the implantation layer.
explanation.e: The perimetrium is the outer uterine covering and cannot support implantation.

subject: Embryology

statement: Which structure must degenerate for blastocyst implantation to occur?

explanation.e: Degeneration of the zona pellucida allows “hatching” of the blastocyst so trophoblast cells can attach to the endometrial epithelium for implantation.
explanation.a: Corona radiata cells are dispersed before fertilization and are not the barrier preventing implantation.
explanation.b: Cytotrophoblast forms part of the trophoblast and is essential for implantation rather than degenerating.
explanation.c: The functional layer of endometrium receives the implanting blastocyst and does not degenerate beforehand.
explanation.d: Syncytiotrophoblast actively invades the endometrium during implantation and must remain functional.

subject: Embryology

statement: The seven day blastocyst:

explanation.c: By day 7 the blastocyst has attached to the endometrial epithelium, initiating implantation.
explanation.a: The primitive streak develops during week 3, not in a seven day blastocyst.
explanation.b: The amniotic cavity appears slightly later during the second week.
explanation.d: Chorionic villi have not yet formed at day 7.
explanation.e: The zona pellucida has already degenerated before implantation begins.

subject: Embryology

statement: First sign of pregnancy on ultrasound is the presence of:

explanation.c: The earliest detectable ultrasonographic sign of pregnancy is the intrauterine gestation sac.
explanation.a: The embryonic fetus becomes visible later in development.
explanation.b: Fetal heart movement appears after the gestational sac is identified.
explanation.d: The intrauterine yolk sac develops after the gestational sac is seen.
explanation.e: Placental circulation is established later and is not the first ultrasound sign.

subject: Embryology

statement: At what location does the amniotic cavity develop:

explanation.c: The amniotic cavity develops as a fluid-filled space within the epiblast during the second week.
explanation.a: The trophoblastic layers do not contain the developing amniotic cavity.
explanation.b: The cavity does not form between endoderm and mesoderm.
explanation.d: Extraembryonic mesoderm contributes to chorionic structures, not the amniotic cavity origin.
explanation.e: Hypoblast forms the yolk sac lining rather than the amniotic cavity.

subject: Embryology

statement: Which part of blastocyst gives rise to embryo:

explanation.c: The embryoblast (inner cell mass) forms the embryo proper.
explanation.a: Chorionic mesoderm forms fetal part of placenta, not embryo.
explanation.b: Cytotrophoblast contributes to trophoblastic layers, not embryo.
explanation.d: Extraembryonic mesoderm forms supporting membranes only.
explanation.e: Syncytiotrophoblast forms invasive placental layer, not embryo.

subject: Embryology

statement: The developing embryo has a distinct human appearance by the end of:

explanation.d: By week 8, organogenesis is complete and human features are distinct.
explanation.a: Week 5 still shows early limb and facial bud development.
explanation.b: Week 6 features are still embryologically primitive.
explanation.c: Week 7 shows continued differentiation but not full appearance.
explanation.e: Week 9 is fetal period, after appearance is already established.

subject: Embryology
topic: Weeks 4-8 embryonic folding & germ layer derivatives
tags: Weeks 4-8: Embryonic Folding & Germ Layer Derivatives

statement: At the end of week 2 of development (day 14), what is the composition of the embryonic disk:

explanation.c: By day 14 the embryonic disk is bilaminar, consisting of epiblast and hypoblast.
explanation.a: Definitive ectoderm and endoderm are established after gastrulation in week 3.
explanation.b: All three germ layers are not present until gastrulation occurs.
explanation.d: Hypoblast is also present at the end of week 2.
explanation.e: Mesoderm has not yet formed by day 14.

subject: Embryology
topic: Weeks 4-8 embryonic folding & germ layer derivatives
tags: Weeks 4-8: Embryonic Folding & Germ Layer Derivatives

statement: Which germ layers are present at the end of week 3 of development (day 21):

explanation.b: By day 21 gastrulation has produced the trilaminar embryonic disk composed of ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.
explanation.a: Mesoderm is also present by the end of week 3.
explanation.c: Epiblast and hypoblast characterize the bilaminar disk of week 2.
explanation.d: The embryonic disk is no longer composed solely of epiblast.
explanation.e: Ectoderm is also fully established at this stage.

subject: Embryology
topic: Weeks 4-8 embryonic folding & germ layer derivatives
tags: Weeks 4-8: Embryonic Folding & Germ Layer Derivatives

statement: The epiblast is capable of forming which germ layers:

explanation.d: Cells of the epiblast give rise to all three definitive germ layers during gastrulation.
explanation.a: Mesoderm is also derived from migrating epiblast cells.
explanation.b: Endoderm also originates from the epiblast.
explanation.c: The epiblast forms far more than ectoderm alone.
explanation.e: Epiblast additionally forms ectoderm.

topic: Weeks 4-8 embryonic folding & germ layer derivatives
